:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Suppose we have two vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b},$ given by

$$
\begin{aligned}a & ={a}_{1}i+{a}_{2}j+{a}_{3}k \\ b & ={b}_{1}i+{b}_{2}j+{b}_{3}k.\end{aligned}
$$

The cross product $\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf b$ can be calculated using the following determinant:

$$
\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} & {a}_{3} \\ {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} & {b}_{3}\end{aligned}
$$

For instance, suppose that we have the two vectors $\mathbf{a} = \langle 2,-1,5 \rangle$, $\mathbf{b} = \langle -1,4,2 \rangle$. We can find the cross product of $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}a\times b & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 2 & -1 & 5 \\ -1 & 4 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-1 & 5 \\ 4 & 2\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}2 & 5 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 4\end{aligned}|k \\  & =((-1)\cdot 2-5\cdot 4)i-(2\cdot 2-5\cdot (-1))j+(2\cdot 4-(-1)\cdot (-1))k \\  & =-22i-9j+7k \\  & =⟨-22,-9,7⟩\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Using the determinant formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}a\times b & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 3 & -4 & 1 \\ -7 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-4 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ -7 & 2\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}3 & -4 \\ -7 & 0\end{aligned}|k \\  & =((-4)\cdot 2-1\cdot 0)i-(3\cdot 2-1\cdot (-7))j+(3\cdot 0-(-4)\cdot (-7))k \\  & =-8i-13j-28k \\  & =⟨-8,-13,-28⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Calculating the Cross Product Using Determinants

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Using the determinant formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}a\times b & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 3 & 1 & 2x \\ 0 & 1 & x\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 2x \\ 1 & x\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}3 & 2x \\ 0 & x\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|k \\  & =-xi-3xj+3k \\  & =⟨-x,-3x,3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, computing the magnitude, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}|\,a\times b\,| & =\sqrt{(-x)^{2}+(-3x)^{2}+{3}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{10{x}^{2}+9}.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we solve for $x$ the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned} & |\,a\times b\,|=\sqrt{19} \\  & \sqrt{10{x}^{2}+9}=\sqrt{19} \\  & 10{x}^{2}+9=19 \\  & 10{x}^{2}=10 \\  & {x}^{2}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $x= \pm 1.$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Solving for an Unknown in an Equation Involving the Cross Product

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
We have been using the following formula to compute the cross product of two vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}a\times b & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} & {a}_{3} \\ {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} & {b}_{3}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} & {a}_{3} \\ {b}_{2} & {b}_{3}\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} & {a}_{3} \\ {b}_{1} & {b}_{3}\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ {b}_{1} & {b}_{2}\end{aligned}|k \\  & =({a}_{2}{b}_{3}-{a}_{3}{b}_{2})i-({a}_{1}{b}_{3}-{a}_{3}{b}_{1})j+({a}_{1}{b}_{2}-{a}_{2}{b}_{1})k\end{aligned}
$$

But where does this formula come from? Let's find out.

Suppose we want to find the cross product $\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}$ for $\mathbf{a}=a_1\mathbf{i}+a_2\mathbf{j}+a_3\mathbf{k}$ and $\mathbf{b}=b_1\mathbf{i}+b_2\mathbf{j}+b_3\mathbf{k}.$ Using properties of the cross product, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}a\times b & =({a}_{1}i+{a}_{2}j+{a}_{3}k)\times ({b}_{1}i+{b}_{2}j+{b}_{3}k) \\  & =({a}_{1}\cdot {b}_{1})i\times i+({a}_{1}\cdot {b}_{2})i\times j+({a}_{1}\cdot {b}_{3})i\times k \\  & +({a}_{2}\cdot {b}_{1})j\times i+({a}_{2}\cdot {b}_{2})j\times j+({a}_{2}\cdot {b}_{3})j\times k \\  & +({a}_{3}\cdot {b}_{1})k\times i+({a}_{3}\cdot {b}_{2})k\times j+({a}_{3}\cdot {b}_{3})k\times k.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the cross product of two parallel (collinear) vectors is equal to $\mathbf 0,$ we have

$$
\mathbf{i}\times\mathbf{i} = \mathbf{j}\times\mathbf{j} = \mathbf{k}\times\mathbf{k} = \mathbf 0.
$$

Also, using the definition of the cross product we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}i\times j=k, & \,j\times i=-k, \\ j\times k=i, & \,k\times j=-i, \\ k\times i=j, & \,i\times k=-j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}a\times b & =({a}_{1}\cdot {b}_{1}){{i\times i}_{⏟}}_{=0}+({a}_{1}\cdot {b}_{2}){{i\times j}_{⏟}}_{=k}+({a}_{1}\cdot {b}_{3}){{i\times k}_{⏟}}_{=-j} \\  & +({a}_{2}\cdot {b}_{1}){{j\times i}_{⏟}}_{=-k}+({a}_{2}\cdot {b}_{2}){{j\times j}_{⏟}}_{=0}+({a}_{2}\cdot {b}_{3}){{j\times k}_{⏟}}_{=i} \\  & +({a}_{3}\cdot {b}_{1}){{k\times i}_{⏟}}_{=j}+({a}_{3}\cdot {b}_{2}){{k\times j}_{⏟}}_{=-i}+({a}_{3}\cdot {b}_{3}){{k\times k}_{⏟}}_{=0} \\  & =({a}_{2}{b}_{3}-{a}_{3}{b}_{2})i-({a}_{1}{b}_{3}-{a}_{3}{b}_{1})j+({a}_{1}{b}_{2}-{a}_{2}{b}_{1})k.\end{aligned}
$$

The expression above is equal to the formula given for the cross product of two general vectors using the determinant.
